question: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of right-sided facial weakness and sound intolerance. Three days ago, he hit the right side of his head in a motor vehicle collision. He neither lost consciousness nor sought medical attention. Physical examination shows drooping of the mouth and ptosis on the right side. Sensation over the face is not impaired. Impedance audiometry shows an absence of the acoustic reflex in the right ear. Which of the following muscles is most likely paralyzed in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Motor vehicle collision -> head trauma -> right-sided facial weakness and sound intolerance -> right facial nerve involvement -> facial nerve paralysis -> drooping of the mouth and ptosis on the right side -> 90%
enhanced_information: The most likely paralyzed muscle in this patient is the Tensor tympani due to right facial nerve involvement following head trauma, leading to facial nerve paralysis with drooping of the mouth and ptosis on the right side. The evidence paths confirming the relationship between facial nerve structure and symptoms like blepharoptosis support this conclusion.
analysis: The core medical principle here is to consider the presentation of right-sided facial weakness and sound intolerance following head trauma, indicating facial nerve involvement. Given the symptoms of drooping of the mouth and ptosis on the right side, along with the absence of the acoustic reflex in the right ear, the most likely paralyzed muscle in this patient is the Tensor tympani.
